R05-E-01: A recurring complaint about modern money holds that it lost its integrity when it ceased to be tied to gold. On this view, a currency backed by metal disciplines governments: they cannot issue what they do not hold, and so savers are protected from the slow erosion of their wealth by inflation. The appeal is easy to understand, since gold is tangible, scarce and ancient, while paper notes and electronic balances seem by comparison to be mere promises, and promises can be broken. Yet the discipline the gold standard imposed was less a protection than a transfer of risk. Under a metallic standard, the quantity of money depended on the pace of mining and on the flow of metal between countries, neither of which had much to do with the needs of trade. When output grew faster than the stock of gold, prices had to fall, and falling prices are hard on anyone who owes money. A farmer who borrowed against next year's harvest found that the harvest fetched less while the sum he owed stayed exactly the same. Long stretches of gold discipline were therefore stretches in which debtors, who were usually the less wealthy, bore much of the cost of keeping money sound for their creditors. Nor did the standard remove discretion from governments as completely as its admirers suggest. Countries suspended convertibility during wars and crises, altered the official price of gold, and managed their reserves with a good deal of judgement. The rule held while it was convenient and was set aside when it was not; what it chiefly removed was the ability to respond to a slump without first abandoning the rule itself, and many economic historians have observed that, in the depression of the 1930s, the countries that left gold earlier tended to recover earlier. None of this means that the nostalgia is groundless. Its real object is not the metal but trust: people want assurance that whoever controls money will not debase it for short-term ends. That is a legitimate demand, and governments have given it plenty of justification, but it is better met by institutions whose conduct can be observed, questioned and corrected than by tying the supply of money to the accidents of geology. Gold offers the comfort of a rule that no one made; the difficulty is that a rule no one made is also a rule that no one can sensibly adjust when circumstances change.
R05-E-02: Insurance works by pooling: many people each pay a modest premium so that the few who suffer a loss can be compensated, and the arrangement rests on a fact that is easy to overlook: no one in the pool knows in advance who the unlucky will be. If the pool holds a mixture of people whose risks differ but cannot be told apart, a single price can cover everyone, and the careful and the careless alike buy protection they value. The trouble begins when buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer does. Those who expect to claim find a uniform premium a bargain; those who expect not to find it expensive, and some of them leave. The insurer, seeing claims rise relative to premiums, raises the price, which drives out the next group of relatively safe customers. In the extreme case the pool shrinks until only the riskiest remain, and a product that many people would have wanted cannot be sold at a price that anyone else will pay. Economists call this unravelling adverse selection, and it can happen even though no one has lied to anyone. Two remedies are available, and neither is free. The first is for insurers to close the gap in information through medical examinations, questionnaires and records of past claims. Each of these helps, yet each also wears away the pooling that made insurance worth having, because a pool sorted precisely by risk is no longer sharing much risk at all. A person found to have a costly condition before buying cover will be quoted a premium close to the expected cost of treating it, which is to say no insurance in any useful sense. The second remedy is to make membership compulsory or nearly universal, so that the low-risk cannot walk away. This keeps the pool mixed, but it asks the healthy to subsidise the sick on terms that some of them did not choose and regard as unfair. The choice between these remedies is often presented as a technical matter for actuaries, but it is better understood as a choice about how much of life's bad luck a society wishes to share. For risks that people largely take on by choice, such as a dangerous hobby, pricing by risk seems fair enough. For risks that arrive at birth or by pure chance, sorting begins to look like penalising people twice: once through fate, and again through the price.
R05-E-03: Imagine a small-town bank that is entirely sound: its loans are prudent and its borrowers will repay, although those loans run for years while its deposits can be withdrawn on any day. Suppose a rumour spreads that this institution is in trouble. Each depositor now faces a simple calculation: if others withdraw and I do not, my bank may have to sell its loans in a hurry and at a loss, leaving me with little, whereas if I withdraw first, I lose nothing. It is therefore rational to run whether or not the rumour is true, and once enough people run, the rumour becomes true. Such a bank fails not because it was unsound but because it was believed to be. Deposit insurance is the classic answer, because a guarantee from the state, up to some limit, alters the calculation entirely. A depositor who stays put loses nothing even if her bank collapses, so she has no reason to join a run, and because no one runs, the guarantee is seldom called upon. Seen in this light, insurance looks almost like a free lunch: a promise that, by being believed, makes its own fulfilment unnecessary. The objection is familiar. Insured depositors have no reason to ask what their bank does with their money, and a bank whose depositors do not ask can take risks that it would otherwise have to justify to them. The guarantee that ends panics may thus encourage the very recklessness that makes failures likely. Critics conclude that deposit insurance trades a visible problem for a hidden one, and some would scale it back so that depositors once again have a reason to pay attention. The objection is sound as far as it goes, but it rests on a curious picture of who disciplined banks before guarantees existed. Ordinary depositors were never skilled readers of loan books; what they were skilled at was panic. The discipline they supplied was indiscriminate, striking prudent and imprudent banks without distinction once fear took hold, as the town bank illustrates. If insured depositors stop watching, little genuine scrutiny is lost, and the task passes to those equipped for it: supervisors with the power to inspect, and the large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake. The lesson of the objection is not that guarantees are a mistake but that they must be paired with oversight, and that the limit on cover matters a great deal, since it decides who still has a reason to care.
R05-E-04: Long before there were central banks, people understood that a ruler who clipped the edges of coins, or mixed base metal into silver, was taking a share of his subjects' wealth without asking them. The modern version of the idea holds that a government which finances its spending by creating money imposes an inflation tax on everyone who holds that money. No law is passed and no collector calls; the price of bread simply rises, and the real value of the cash in people's pockets falls in proportion. In one respect the analogy with taxation is exact: resources move from the public to the issuer of money, who has spent the new money before its effect on prices is felt. Critics of this practice argue that it is worse than ordinary taxation precisely because it is hidden: a tax on incomes must be proposed, debated and voted upon; an inflation tax requires only that the issuing authority do nothing to stop it. It also tends to fall heavily on those least able to protect themselves, such as households that keep their savings in cash or depend on incomes fixed in money terms, while it benefits anyone whose debts shrink in real value as prices rise. Among the largest such debtors, of course, is often the state itself. The analogy misleads, however, when it is pressed too far. A tax is a deliberate choice, whereas much inflation arises from events that no government chose, such as a failed harvest, a war in a distant region or a sudden jump in the price of fuel. Moreover, where most money takes the form of bank deposits that pay interest, and where that interest rises when inflation rises, the revenue a state gains from mild inflation is modest. To describe every increase in prices as a tax is to attribute intention and gain in cases where there may be neither. What the old idea gets right is the question it trains us to ask: who gains? When inflation is high and persistent and the state is a heavy debtor, the answer frequently points to the treasury, and the language of taxation is then not rhetoric but accurate description. When inflation is mild, or arrives from abroad through the price of imports, the same language obscures more than it reveals. The concept of an inflation tax is best treated as a tool of diagnosis rather than as a verdict reached in advance.
R05-E-05: The case for an independent central bank is usually made in terms of temptation. Elected governments face voters at regular intervals, and before an election they are tempted to loosen money, buying a brief rise in output and employment at the price of higher inflation later. Because the public comes to anticipate this, it builds the expected inflation into wages and prices in advance, so that the boost to output never materialises and only the inflation remains. Handing monetary policy to an appointed body with a mandate for stable prices removes the temptation and makes promises of low inflation believable. The gain, on this account, lies in credibility rather than in any superior cleverness on the part of the officials. Against this stands a democratic objection that is easy to underrate. Decisions about interest rates have large effects on the distribution of income and wealth, between borrowers and savers, between the owners of assets and those who live on wages, and between one region and another. In a democracy, choices with consequences of that kind are supposed to be made by people who can be removed at the ballot box. To delegate them, the objection runs, is to take out of public contest exactly the decisions that most need it. Both positions are partly right, and the distance between them narrows once we ask what, precisely, has been delegated. Independence in the choice of instruments is not the same as independence in the choice of goals. A legislature can fix the target, an inflation rate for instance, and require the central bank to explain in public whenever it misses; that body then decides how to reach the target, and it alone sets the interest rate. This arrangement preserves the commitment that defeats electoral temptation while leaving the ends of policy with elected representatives, and it answers much of the democratic objection without surrendering the gain in credibility. The settlement is stable, however, only while the mandate remains narrow. When central banks are asked in addition to secure financial stability, support employment, steer credit towards favoured sectors or manage the risks of a changing climate, the claim that they merely apply technical means to democratically chosen ends begins to wear thin, because deciding how to trade these goals off against one another is itself a political judgement. The more a central bank is asked to do, the weaker its claim to be left alone while doing it.
R05-E-06: Debt is described, almost everywhere, in moral vocabulary. We speak of honouring our debts and of meeting our obligations, while default is treated as a failure of character and the borrower who cannot pay is presumed to have been improvident. These words are old, and they carry the experience of every society that has had to persuade strangers to trust one another across time. The language is not wholly misplaced, since a promise to repay is a promise, and a society in which such promises were lightly broken would soon find that no one would lend at all. The moral framing, however, assigns the whole of the responsibility to one side of what is a two-sided contract. A loan is made by a lender who chose to lend, who estimated the chance of not being repaid and built that chance into the rate of interest, and who has been paid, in that higher rate, for bearing exactly the risk that sometimes comes to pass. When a borrower defaults, the risk for which the lender was compensated has simply materialised. To treat default as a sin rather than as an outcome the contract foresaw is to let lenders collect the premium for risk while disowning the risk itself. This asymmetry has practical consequences. Where the moral framing is strong, lenders come under less pressure to judge carefully whether a borrower can repay, since any failure will be laid at the borrower's door, and borrowers in difficulty may conceal their distress out of shame instead of seeking to renegotiate early, when a settlement would cost both parties least. A lender that knows blame will travel in only one direction has in effect been relieved of part of the cost of its own mistakes, and an institution relieved of that cost can be expected to make more of them. The bankruptcy law of many countries embodies a different view: it treats a fresh start for an honest debtor as a social good, partly on the practical ground that a person crushed by debts that can never be paid produces little for anyone, creditors included. None of this licenses casual default, and a borrower who spends money he never meant to return has done wrong in the plainest sense. The point is that obligation runs in both directions: the borrower owes repayment, and the lender owes care in deciding to lend. A moral language that recognised both duties would not be softer than the one we have; it would simply be more accurate about where responsibility lies when a loan goes bad.
R05-E-07: When a market collapses, the verdict arrives quickly: it was a bubble, and those who bought near the top were caught up in a collective madness. The diagnosis is comforting, because it implies that the error was obvious and that sober people would have avoided it. It is also, in a great many cases, a judgement that could have been made only afterwards. A price that later falls by three quarters was not necessarily irrational when it was paid; it may have been a reasonable wager on an outcome that simply did not occur. Consider the shares of firms built around a genuinely new technology. No one knows at the outset which of them will dominate, how large the market will become, or how long any dominance will last. A high price for the whole group can reflect the small chance of an enormous success for one or two of its members, and when most of them then fail, the collapse in prices is consistent with the original bet having been a sensible one. Hindsight converts uncertainty into folly by forgetting that the winners were not known in advance. The same consideration explains why confident announcements that a bubble is under way have such a mixed record, since prices have sometimes gone on rising for years after the warning was issued. None of this shows that bubbles are a myth. Something does distinguish a bubble from a failed bet, but it is not the size of the eventual fall; it is the reason for which the asset was bought. A buyer who pays a high price because she believes the asset will yield returns that justify it is making a wager that may be mistaken but is not speculative in the narrow sense. A buyer who pays the price only because he expects someone else to pay more, and who would not hold the asset on its own merits for a day, is taking part in something of a different kind: a chain whose value depends on recruiting a next buyer, and which must at some point break. The difficulty is that this distinguishing mark lies in motives, and prices do not record motives. Two buyers paying the same price on the same day may be doing quite different things, and an observer who sees only the price cannot tell how much of a market consists of believers and how much of passers-on. That is why proposals that regulators should identify bubbles as they form and deflate them, by raising interest rates or restricting purchases, ask for a judgement that is rarely available in time, and why such measures, if applied, are likely to fall on sound and unsound investments alike. A more modest aim is within reach. What turns the collapse of a price into a wider calamity is usually not the fall itself but the borrowing that financed the purchases, because losses on borrowed money pass from the buyer to the lender, and from the lender to everyone who depends on it. Limits on leverage do not require anyone to know whether a price is justified; they require only that whoever turns out to be wrong should be wrong mainly with his own money. This is less dramatic than a promise to prick bubbles before they grow, and it will disappoint those who want the next crash prevented rather than contained, but a rule that works without foresight has the considerable merit of not depending on a capacity that no one possesses. Such a policy does not aim to prevent bubbles. It aims to make them survivable.
R05-E-08: The textbook account of banking runs roughly as follows. Savers deposit money; a bank keeps a fraction of each deposit as reserves and lends out the rest; the borrower spends the loan, the recipient deposits it at another bank, which in turn lends out most of it, and so on, until the original deposit has been multiplied by a factor that depends on the fraction held back. On this account banks are intermediaries, passing the savings of some people on to the projects of others, and the quantity of money in an economy is ultimately governed by the central bank's control over the quantity of reserves. As a description of what actually happens when a loan is made, this has the sequence backwards. A bank that approves a loan does not hand over notes taken from a vault of accumulated deposits; it credits the borrower's account with a new deposit, and the money the borrower then spends did not exist a moment earlier. Lending creates deposits rather than the reverse. What limits a lender is therefore not a pool of prior savings but its judgement of whether a loan will be repaid at a profit, the capital it must hold against possible losses, the demand from creditworthy borrowers, and the price at which it can obtain the reserves needed to settle payments with other banks, a price that the central bank sets through the rate of interest rather than through the quantity of reserves. The textbook is not simply wrong. A single bank that lends freely will soon find its new deposits draining away as borrowers pay people who bank elsewhere, and it must then attract deposits or borrow reserves to cover the outflow; from the standpoint of one institution, lending does seem to require funding. The error lies in generalising from the single bank to the system. What is a drain for one bank is an inflow for another, and the system as a whole is constrained less by the deposits it has gathered than by the willingness of banks to lend and of borrowers to borrow. The difference matters for policy. If the multiplier story were right, a central bank that supplied banks with abundant reserves would set off a roughly proportionate expansion of lending. On the alternative account, when borrowers are cautious and banks are worried about losses, additional reserves may simply sit unused, because nothing in the decision to lend was waiting for them. Arguments about why lending has stalled are then better directed at the demand for credit and the condition of banks' balance sheets than at the quantity of reserves. A further implication is drawn less often. If banks merely passed on existing savings, the direction of their lending would be a secondary matter, a question of how efficiently funds that already exist are placed. If instead banks create money when they lend, then their decisions about whom to lend to determine what new purchasing power enters the economy, and where. A boom in lending against existing houses and a boom in lending to firms that build new things both enlarge the supply of money, yet they do very different things with it: the first mainly raises the price of what is already there, while the second adds to what there is. Banking, on this view, is not a neutral pipe between savers and borrowers but one of the principal means by which a society decides what its new money will be used for.
